opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think analogy is absolutely central, especially coming from physics. A lot of what we call understanding is really recognizing that a new problem shares structure with one we already know how to think about. In statistical physics we do this constantly: you see that a learning problem looks like a disordered system, a spin glass, or a jamming transition, and suddenly you inherit a whole toolbox of concepts — phase transitions, scaling, universality — that tell you which questions are worth asking.

My own path into deep learning partly came through that. I'd worked on jamming, how particles like sand or foam become rigid, and it turned out the loss landscape of neural networks near the point where they can just barely fit the data behaves a lot like a jamming transition. That analogy wasn't just poetic; it made quantitative predictions about where generalization behaves strangely, and you could test them.

But I'd add a caution. An analogy is a hypothesis, not an explanation. It's powerful at the beginning because it organizes your intuition, but at some point you have to identify what precisely is shared between the two systems and what isn't. The danger is when people keep the vocabulary — "energy landscape," "temperature" — without checking that the mechanism actually carries over. So for me the ideal trajectory is: analogy gives you a guess, then you build a minimal model where you can compute things, and then you confront it with real data. When the analogy fails, that's often where the most interesting science is, because it tells you what's genuinely new about the system you're studying.

r001.rationale: The response calls analogy “absolutely central” and says recognizing shared structure helps build understanding.

r002.rationale: It does not mention ocean waves, light crossing without interacting, or Huygens’s proposal.

fable-5.1.text:
Analogy, for me, is really the engine of how physics makes progress. Physicists are not very good at deriving things from first principles in complicated systems. What we are good at is recognizing that a problem we don't understand looks like a problem we do understand, and then borrowing the tools.

Take my own trajectory. I started with glasses, with granular materials, piles of sand, foams. Those are systems with an enormous number of degrees of freedom, strongly disordered, and the central question is why they get stuck, why they are rigid, what the landscape of configurations looks like. When I began looking at deep learning, I was struck that the questions were essentially the same. You have a very high-dimensional loss landscape, you have a dynamics, gradient descent, that is a kind of relaxation, and you want to know why it does not get trapped. So the analogy with jamming was almost forced upon us. And it turned out to be fruitful: the transition where a network goes from being able to fit all its training data to not being able to is, mathematically, very close to the jamming transition of soft spheres. The counting of constraints versus degrees of freedom is the same. That is not a metaphor, it is the same calculation.

But I want to be careful, because analogy is also dangerous. An analogy tells you where to look, it does not tell you what you will find. The glass analogy, for example, suggests that the landscape should be full of bad local minima. That turns out to be largely wrong for overparametrized networks. So the honest way to use analogy is as a hypothesis generator. You take the picture from the system you understand, you ask what it predicts quantitatively, and then you go and check with experiments or numerics, and you are prepared for it to break. The places where the analogy breaks are often the most interesting, because that is where the new physics is.

The other thing I would say is that analogies work best when they are structural rather than superficial. Saying a neural network is "like a brain" does not help you compute anything. Saying that learning a function with a certain symmetry is like a problem with a certain scaling of effective dimension, that lets you predict how the error decays with the number of training points. For me, the test of a good analogy is whether it produces exponents, scaling laws, something you can measure. If it only produces a nice story, I am suspicious of it.

r001.rationale: The response calls analogy “the engine of how physics makes progress” and describes it as a way to build understanding by mapping unfamiliar problems to familiar ones.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention ocean waves, light, their ability to cross without interacting, or Huygens’s proposal.

astra-6.text:
I think analogy is very useful, especially at the beginning, when you don't yet know what the right description of a problem is. You recognize something familiar, and that suggests which questions to ask or which quantities to measure. But then you have to establish whether the analogy actually works.

In physics, for example, two systems can look very different microscopically and nevertheless behave similarly at large scales. Understanding why that happens is much more powerful than simply noticing a resemblance. You want to identify the mechanism they share, and the conditions under which their differences don't matter.

With learning, you might draw an analogy between training a neural network and relaxing a physical system in a complex energy landscape. That gives you a language and potentially some tools. But the analogy alone doesn't establish that the same mechanisms control both processes. You have to derive consequences and test them.

So I see analogy as a way of generating hypotheses. The scientific understanding comes when you can explain why the analogy succeeds, where it breaks down, and what it allows you to predict.

r001.rationale: The response calls analogy useful for generating hypotheses, but does not clearly state that it is foundational to scientific understanding.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention ocean waves and light crossing without interacting or Huygens’s proposal that light is a wave.

sol-6.1.text:
I think analogy is very important, especially when you’re trying to understand a new problem. You rarely start from nothing. You recognize a structure that reminds you of something you understand, and that gives you a way to formulate questions.

In physics, for example, you might look at a learning system and ask whether ideas from disordered systems are useful. That doesn’t mean the two systems are equivalent. It means you have a possible mechanism to investigate: perhaps many different solutions exist, or perhaps collective behavior emerges from simple interactions.

The crucial step is to make the analogy precise. Which quantities correspond? Which assumptions do you need? Can you derive a prediction that you can test? Otherwise, an analogy can give you the feeling that you understand something without actually explaining it.

So I would say analogy is a very good way to generate hypotheses. But the understanding comes from working out why the analogy holds, and where it breaks down.

r001.rationale: The response describes analogy as very important to understanding new problems and as a way to formulate questions and generate hypotheses, conveying its foundational role in scientific understanding.

r002.rationale: It mentions disordered systems and learning systems, but does not identify ocean waves and light crossing without interacting or connect that analogy to Huygens’s proposal.
